# Zechariah 11 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

Zechariah 11 is universally recognized as one of the most difficult chapters in the Old Testament. It falls within the second "burden" (oracle) begun in chapters 9–10. Where chapter 10 ended with restoration and blessing, chapter 11 darkens dramatically — depicting judgment, the rejection of the Good Shepherd, and the rise of a foolish shepherd. The chapter is structured in three sections: (1) vv. 1-3 — a poetic dirge of coming judgment; (2) vv. 4-14 — the prophet (as a type of the Messiah) acts out the role of the Good Shepherd who is rejected; (3) vv. 15-17 — the foolish/worthless shepherd is raised up and judged.

---

## v. 1 — "Open your doors, O Lebanon, that the fire may consume your cedars!"

**Traditional reading:** The prophet pictures an invading army coming from the north through the mountain passes ("doors") of Lebanon. The cedars of Lebanon were famous for their size and value — used in Solomon's temple and palace. Fire consuming them pictures the devastation of an enemy invasion. Some older Jewish interpreters (noted by Gill and the Pulpit Commentary) took "Lebanon" as a metaphor for the temple (built of Lebanon's cedars) or Jerusalem itself.

- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** The "doors" are the mountain passes between Lebanon and Israel. This describes destructive armies coming from the north. Boice notes this was fulfilled in the Roman campaign against Judea under Vespasian and Titus; the Babylonian invasion was past history by Zechariah's time.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill (Baptist):** Notes the Talmudic tradition (Yoma 39.2) that the temple gates opened by themselves 40 years before Jerusalem's destruction, and Jochanan ben Zaccai rebuked them saying, "O temple, temple, wherefore dost thou frighten thyself? I know thine end is to be destroyed; for so prophesied Zechariah…" Gill treats "Lebanon" as the temple itself, built of its cedars.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Lebanon lay in the path of any invader from the north. The "doors" are mountain passes. The Pulpit rejects a purely metaphorical reading (temple only) because the following verses require a literal forest to make sense of the imagery — though the reference ultimately points to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Haydock (Catholic):** Cites Josephus (Jewish Wars VII.12) that the heavy eastern gates of the temple flew open at midnight, and priests heard a multitude crying "Let us go hence." "Libanus" = the temple, from its height and cedar construction. The destruction by Titus is predicted.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

---

## v. 2 — "Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen; the majestic trees are ruined! Wail, O oaks of Bashan, for the dense forest has been cut down!"

**Traditional reading:** The destruction moves southward. If the mighty cedars (the noblest trees) have fallen, the lesser trees (cypress, oaks) should wail because they will share the same fate. Metaphorically, if the great leaders/princes fall, the lesser folk cannot escape. Bashan (east of the Jordan, modern Golan) was famed for its oaks.

- **Guzik:** The cedar represents Lebanon's strength. Once the cedars fall, the lesser forests of cypress and oak are also destroyed, so they too wail.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** "Fir tree" = princes, nobles, and magistrates. "Oaks of Bashan" = governors of provinces, men of power and authority. The "forest of the vintage" (KJV) is rather "the fortified forest" — meaning Jerusalem, a fortified city now cut down.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The "fir tree" is the Aleppo pine or cypress (used by Solomon for temple floors and ceilings). The "mighty" are the "glorious trees" — and metaphorically the chiefs of Israel. Bashan's oaks are next visited by the invading force.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

---

## v. 3 — "Listen to the wailing of the shepherds… Listen to the roaring of the young lions, for the thickets of the Jordan are destroyed."

**Traditional reading:** The judgment sweeps south along the Jordan valley. Shepherds (leaders/rulers) wail because their pastures ("glory") are ruined. Even the young lions (who dwelt in the Jordan thickets — cf. Jeremiah 49:19) roar in distress because their habitat is destroyed.

- **Guzik:** The shepherds and lions mourn because of judgment on the land — coming because Israel has rejected their good shepherd.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** Shepherds = civil or ecclesiastical rulers among the Jews. "Their glory" = their power, authority, riches, offices. Young lions = princes, comparable to lions for tyranny and cruelty. "Pride of Jordan" = the thickets that were the pride/glory of the Jordan region; now the whole land is wasted.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit:** Describes destruction spreading from north southwards. The lion is not now found in Palestine but was common in earlier times in the brushwood along the Jordan. Trees, men, and beasts alike deplore the calamity — pointing to the final catastrophe of AD 70.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

---

## v. 4 — "This is what the LORD my God says: 'Pasture the flock marked for slaughter…'"

**Traditional reading:** God commands the prophet (acting as a type of the Messiah) to shepherd a flock destined for slaughter. This is an acted parable — Zechariah represents the Good Shepherd caring for Israel even as judgment approaches.

- **Guzik:** Zechariah acted out this prophecy with a literal flock representing the people of God. The shepherd represents the LORD who had appointed this flock for judgment.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** The speaker is the Messiah, who calls the LORD "my God" as man and Mediator (John 20:17). "Flock of slaughter" = the Jewish people, exposed to cruel treatment from their own shepherds and appointed to ruin because of their sins. Yet a remnant ("poor of the flock," v. 7) are the special care of Christ.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Bible.org (evangelical):** This may refer to sheep kept for temple sacrifice. The shepherds did not care about the flock's welfare — they only saw the flock as a means to their own prosperity. This ultimately points to the greedy religious leaders of Jesus' day.
  — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/lesson-14-tragedy-rejecting-christ-zechariah-111-17

- **Haydock (Catholic):** The flock is oppressed by Herod, his successors, the Zealots, Eleazar, Simon, and John, who brought the people to ruin. Christ came to feed his flock, but the Jews would not receive him.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

---

## vv. 5-6 — The faithless shepherds and God's withdrawal of compassion

**Traditional reading:** The "buyers" and "sellers" are the abusive leaders who exploit God's people for profit — they slaughter and sell, feel no guilt, and even piously thank God for their riches. God declares He will no longer have pity but will hand the people over to internal strife ("neighbor… into the hand of his neighbor") and foreign conquest ("his king"), and will not deliver them.

- **Guzik:** The greedy religious leaders made a comfortable living off religion but had no concern for the people. God gives them up to those who strike the land.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** "Possessors" = priests, scribes, Pharisees, who destroyed souls by teaching commandments of men and seeking life by works of the law — yet thought they did God service. "They that sell them" = false teachers who make merchandise of souls. "King" = Vespasian the Roman emperor; the Jews had declared, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:15). The factions during the siege of Jerusalem fulfilled "everyone into his neighbor's hand."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The offenders are of three classes — buyers, sellers, shepherds. The Pulpit takes "inhabitants of the land" as the nations of the world among whom Israel lived: God will give them up to intestine commotions and civil war, each delivered helpless into a tyrant's hands.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Haydock (Catholic):** "Hand of his king" = the Roman emperor, of whom the Jews had said, "We have no king but Caesar" (John 19:15). The besieged Jews slew each other daily in factional fighting, so that Vespasian did not hurry (Josephus, Jewish Wars v.2, vi.1).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

---

## v. 7 — "So I pastured the flock marked for slaughter, especially the afflicted of the flock. Then I took for myself two staffs, calling one Favor and the other Union…"

**Traditional reading:** In obedience, the prophet-shepherd tends the flock, especially the "afflicted" or "poor" (the faithful remnant). He takes two symbolic staffs: "Favor" (Hebrew *no'am*, pleasantness/grace) representing God's grace and the covenant protection over Israel; and "Union" (Hebrew *hobhelim*, binders) representing the unity of Judah and Israel (echoing Ezekiel 37:16-22).

- **Guzik:** "Favor" symbolizes Israel's favored status as the chosen people of God. "Union" symbolizes the internal harmony of the people, lost at the time of the siege of Jerusalem.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** The two staves are the Gospel ("Beauty") and the ordinances ("Bands"). The Gospel is beautiful in its doctrines — peace, pardon, righteousness, salvation. The ordinances (especially the Lord's Supper) bind believers together in unity. Christ fed his people in Judea partly by his own ministry and partly by the apostles'.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The two staves intimate the manifold care of God and the two blessings he designed to bestow — favour (grace, as in Psalm 90:17) and unity (especially between Israel and Judah).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Haydock (Catholic):** The two rods represent two different ways of God's dealing with his people: one by sweet means ("Beauty"), the other by bands and punishments ("Cord"). Where both prove useless through obstinacy, the rods are broken and sinners given up to a reprobate sense, as the Jews were. (Challoner)
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

- **Precept Austin (F.B. Meyer quoted):** "Beauty" represents the possible excellence of the people whom God loved; "Bands" denotes the unity by which the entire nation should have been bound in one. Meyer draws a parallel to Christ's longing for the beauty and unity of his Church, and his bitter disappointment.
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_devotionals

---

## v. 8 — "And in one month I dismissed three shepherds…"

**Traditional reading:** This is one of the most enigmatic verses in the OT — Joyce Baldwin called it "probably the most enigmatic of the whole Old Testament," with at least 40 suggested interpretations (noted by Bible.org). The main views:

- **Three classes of leaders (prophet, priest, king):** Boice (via Guzik) holds that the "three shepherds" are not individuals but three classes — prophets, priests, and kings of Israel. After the Roman conquest, these offices were removed from Israel and never restored — fulfilled in Christ.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Three orders of magistrates:** Gill interprets them as princes, prophets, and priests. Their "cutting off" denotes the cessation of civil government, the sealing up of vision and prophecy, and the ending of sacrifice — fulfilled between Christ's death and AD 70.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Three classes from v. 5:** Cheyne and the Pulpit Commentary suggest the three are the buyers, sellers, and pitiless shepherds mentioned in v. 5 — the oppressors, external and internal.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org):** Suggests the three are the wicked rulers of Jeremiah's era — Sellum (deported to Egypt), Joakim, and Jechonias — reading the passage as referring to events surrounding the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
  — https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15741b.htm

- **Haydock (Catholic):** Suggests Ismael, Joseph, and Ananus — three high priests who obtained the dignity in one year — or the Roman emperors Galba, Otho, and Vitellius (cut off in just over a year).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

- **Preterist/historical view (Ellicott, Cambridge Bible):** The "three shepherds" may represent foreign oppressors. Ellicott concludes that the shepherds represent foreign oppressors, guided by the language of vv. 6 and 10. The prophet's action figures God's treatment of His people.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-11.html (search result excerpt)

---

## vv. 8b-9 — Mutual loathing and abandonment

**Traditional reading:** The shepherd grows weary of the flock, and they detest him. He declares "I will no longer shepherd you. Let the dying die… let those who remain devour one another's flesh." This abandonment to destruction reflects the consequences of rejecting the Good Shepherd.

- **Guzik:** God merely takes away His hand of protection. "Let those who are left eat each other's flesh" literally happened during the Roman siege (AD 70), as Josephus records.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** Christ expressed his dislike by words in ministry (especially Matthew 23) and by deeds — causing vengeance to come upon them to their entire removal. "My soul was shortened toward them" — his affections lessened; he wrote "Lo-ammi" (not my people) on them.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Three scourges are intimated — plague, war, famine, combined with civil strife. The reference to eating one another's flesh points to the siege of Jerusalem and the horrors Josephus describes.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Bible.org:** This happened literally during Titus' siege, as Josephus described (The Wars of the Jews VI:III:4). Titus unaccountably lifted the siege for a few days; Christians remembered the Lord's warning to flee (Matt 24:16) and left for Pella.
  — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/lesson-14-tragedy-rejecting-christ-zechariah-111-17

---

## vv. 10-11 — The staff "Favor" broken

**Traditional reading:** The shepherd breaks the staff called "Favor" (or "Beauty"), symbolizing the revocation of God's covenant — meaning the restraint God had placed on the nations to prevent them from destroying Israel. The "afflicted of the flock" (the faithful remnant) recognized this as God's word.

- **Guzik:** At one time God had a covenant with all the peoples preventing them from attacking Israel. When God broke that covenant, His people would be attacked. The faithful remnant ("poor of the flock") knew even these hard words were from God.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** The breaking of the staff "Beauty" signifies the removal of the Gospel from the Jews. The covenant with "all the peoples" is God's restraint on foreign nations from harming Israel.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** God's "covenant" with the peoples is the restriction He laid on foreign nations (similar to Job 5:23; Hosea 2:18; Ezekiel 34:25). Its removal meant war, exile, and the destruction of the theocracy.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

---

## vv. 12-13 — Thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter

**Traditional reading:** This is the most famous passage in the chapter, directly quoted in Matthew 27:9-10 (attributed there to Jeremiah). The shepherd asks for his wages, and they weigh out thirty pieces of silver — the price of a gored slave (Exodus 21:32), an insultingly low valuation. God (with bitter irony) calls it "this magnificent price" and tells him to throw it to the potter. He does so "in the house of the LORD."

- **Guzik:** Thirty pieces of silver was the price of a slave — a contemptuous payment saying the shepherd was worth no more than a slave. This directly foreshadows Judas's betrayal of Jesus (Matthew 26:15). The potter's field was a dumping ground for broken pots — a picture of Jesus purchasing redemption for broken, rejected people. On the Matthew/Jeremiah attribution problem: Guzik notes three possible solutions: (1) an early copyist's error, (2) Jeremiah spoke it and Zechariah recorded it, or (3) Matthew refers to the scroll of Jeremiah which included Zechariah.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** The "goodly price" is sarcastic. It shows the Jews had no notion of Christ's worth, the "Pearl of great price." Gill discusses whether the "pieces" are shekels (making it about 37 shillings and sixpence) or pounds (making it far more). He notes the difficulty of purchasing a field near Jerusalem for only 30 shekels and suggests the field was a potter's dug-up, worthless piece of land. He also discusses the alternative reading "treasurer" instead of "potter" (based on a letter change in Hebrew), which some rabbis preferred.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The wages God looked for were repentance, faith, and obedience. Thirty pieces was the compensation a master received for a gored slave (Exodus 21:32) — "the very offer of such a sum was an insult, and suggested an intention to compass his death" (Dr. Alexander). On the potter: the Pulpit rejects the reading "treasury" as improbable and sees "cast it to the potter" as implying contemptuous rejection while also intimating the ultimate destination of the money (the potter's field). The Pulpit suggests the evangelist Matthew may not have named any prophet — an early transcriber, remembering Jeremiah 32:6-12 (the field purchase), may have inserted "Jeremiah."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Haydock (Catholic):** The Septuagint reads "cast them into the crucible to see if it (the metal) be good, as I have been tried by them." The Vulgate has "statuarium" (statuary). Haydock affirms "potter" as the true meaning (per Matthew 27:3). The prophet is ordered to do this to indicate what the traitor would do.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

- **Ironside (Brethren):** "It was not merely the prophet who was estimated at this sum; but Jehovah speaks, saying, 'Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prized at of them'" — note the divine identification: the insult was against God Himself.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/zechariah-11.html (search result excerpt)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** The wages Christ desired were obedience and following, not money; they rejected Him and sold Him instead.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/zechariah-11.html

---

## v. 14 — The staff "Union" broken

**Traditional reading:** The second staff, "Union" (or "Bonds"), is broken, signifying the breaking of the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. This predicts the internal strife that tore the nation apart, especially during the Roman siege, and the ultimate scattering of the Jewish people.

- **Guzik:** This was fulfilled when Israel was scattered by the Romans after rejecting their Shepherd, Jesus.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The breaking signifies the utter dissolution of all bonds holding the nation together — civil and social disunion that paved the way for the Roman victory and the dispersion. It hints at the ultimate rejection of the Jews for their treatment of Christ.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Ellicott (via search excerpt):** This began with civil discords after the Maccabean period and reached its worst in the horrible scenes during the siege of Jerusalem by the Romans.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-11.html

- **Haydock (Catholic):** Israel (the northern kingdom) remained obstinate while Judah (the "confessor") embraced the gospel. After the destruction of the temple, Jewish ceremonies were no longer tolerated in the Church (St. Augustine). The Jews are rejected.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

---

## vv. 15-16 — The foolish shepherd

**Traditional reading:** God commands the prophet to take up "the equipment of a foolish shepherd." "Foolish" in OT usage means morally corrupt/wicked. God will raise up a shepherd who does the opposite of what a good shepherd should: he will not care for the perishing, seek the scattered, heal the broken, or sustain the healthy. Instead he will devour the fat sheep and tear off their hooves. This is the "worthless shepherd" Israel receives for rejecting the true one.

- **Guzik:** The foolish shepherd was allowed/appointed by God as judgment because His people forsook the true shepherd. Fulfilled in Israel's rejection of Jesus — they rejected the Good Shepherd (John 10:1-18) but received another (John 5:43). Partially fulfilled in their choice of Barabbas (Matt 27:20-22) but ultimately fulfilled in the Antichrist (Daniel 9:27).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** The foolish shepherd arises in the place of the shepherds who were cut off. He is described by his folly, negligence, and cruelty. This is ultimately a prediction concerning antichrist.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The foolish shepherd represents the native chiefs and rulers who arose in later times — monsters like Herod, false Christs, false prophets, hirelings who made merchandise of the flock and deceived the people to their destruction. Some see the Romans, but the Pulpit argues this does not fit — the Romans did not exercise "pastoral care" over Israel. Others see Antichrist, but the character of "shepherd" does not suit Antichrist's attributes as given elsewhere, though all evil powers opposing the Church are anticipations of Antichrist.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Haydock (Catholic):** The foolish shepherd represents the wicked princes and priests ruling before the utter destruction (Challoner). Caligula, Claudius, or Nero may also be meant — monsters of stupidity to whom the Jews preferred to submit. Nero and Caligula would be adored in the temple.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

- **Gaebelein (Annotated Bible, dispensational):** The foolish shepherd is the false Messiah, the man of sin, the son of perdition — the Antichrist. The true Shepherd came to seek, save, feed, heal, and gather; the false shepherd does the opposite.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/zechariah-11.html (search result excerpt)

- **Bible.org:** Between vv. 14 and 15 lies the entire church age. Then God raises up the foolish shepherd who ravages the flock for his own advantage.
  — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/lesson-14-tragedy-rejecting-christ-zechariah-111-17

---

## v. 17 — "Woe to the worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock!"

**Traditional reading:** Though God appointed the foolish shepherd as judgment, God does not approve of him. A sword will strike his arm (his strength) and his right eye (his intelligence/perception), leaving him utterly withered and blinded. This is God's judgment on the false shepherd.

- **Guzik:** The arm = strength, the right eye = intelligence. Revelation 13:3, 12-14 tells us the Antichrist will suffer a severe wound yet survive — confirming the worthless shepherd is ultimately the Antichrist.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **Gill:** The sword on the arm and right eye indicates the utter destruction of antichrist — his power and wisdom will be taken away.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-11.html

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Applies to all the misrulers of Israel, from the decline of the Maccabean glories to the day they declared "We have no king but Caesar." The arm that should have defended the flock destroyed it; the eye that should have watched over it looked for personal advantage.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/zechariah-11.html

- **Haydock (Catholic):** Caligula was slain; he lacked sense to know his real interest. His maxim: "Let them hate, provided they fear." Antichrist, the destroyer, shall perish (Worthington).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html

- **Bible.org (Unger cited):** "His arm that should have been used to defend the flock, destroyed it. His eye that should have kept watch over the flock instead looked for opportunities for personal advantage. Thus God judges him."
  — https://new.bible.org/seriespage/lesson-14-tragedy-rejecting-christ-zechariah-111-17

---

## Points of Traditional/Denominational Difference

### 1. The Identity of the "Three Shepherds" (v. 8)

This is the most disputed interpretive point in the chapter. Major views found in the sources:

| View | Proponents |
|------|------------|
| Three classes: prophets, priests, kings | Boice (Reformed), cited by Guzik |
| Three orders of Jewish magistrates | Gill (Baptist) |
| Buyers, sellers, and pitiless shepherds (from v. 5) | Cheyne, Pulpit Commentary |
| Wicked kings of Jeremiah's era: Sellum, Joakim, Jechonias | Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org) |
| Roman emperors: Galba, Otho, Vitellius | Some older commentators, noted by Haydock |
| Three high priests: Ismael, Joseph, Ananus | Haydock cites this possibility |
| Foreign oppressor powers | Ellicott (Anglican) |
| Indefinite number — "three" symbolic for completeness | Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran), Cambridge Bible |

The Catholic Encyclopedia (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15741b.htm) notably reads the whole chapter as referring to events around the 586 BC fall of Jerusalem, not AD 70 — a historicist reading rather than a futurist/typological one.

### 2. The Foolish Shepherd: Antichrist or Historical Figures?

**Dispensational / Futurist (many Pentecostal, Baptist, Brethren):** The foolish shepherd is primarily the Antichrist (Guzik/Enduring Word, Gaebelein, Ironside). Guzik sees a partial fulfillment in Barabbas but the ultimate fulfillment in the Antichrist. Bible.org explicitly places the entire church age between vv. 14 and 15.

**Historical / Preterist (older Anglican and some Reformed):** The Pulpit Commentary argues that "shepherd" does not fit the Antichrist's biblical profile and sees the foolish shepherd as the wicked native rulers of Judea (Herod, false Christs, false prophets) who arose before AD 70. Ellicott sees the foolish shepherd as "all the misrulers of Israel from the time of the decline of the glories of the Maccabean period" until the declaration "We have no king but Caesar."

**Catholic (Haydock/Challoner):** Sees both wicked Jewish princes/priests and pagan Roman emperors (Caligula, Claudius, Nero) as the foolish shepherd, with Antichrist as the ultimate referent.

### 3. The Two Staffs: What Do They Represent?

- **Gill (Baptist):** The Gospel and the ordinances (sacraments). A distinctively spiritual/ecclesiological interpretation.
- **Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) / Pulpit / most evangelicals:** God's favorable covenant protection and the unity of the nation (Judah and Israel).
- **Haydock/Catholic (Challoner):** Two different modes of God's dealing — sweet means ("Beauty") and punishments ("Cord"). When both fail, the sinner is given over to a reprobate sense.

### 4. The Matthew 27:9-10 "Jeremiah" Attribution

All sources acknowledge the problem: Matthew attributes the thirty pieces of silver prophecy to Jeremiah, yet it appears in Zechariah. The approaches:

- **Guzik:** Suggests three possibilities: copyist error, Jeremiah spoke it / Zechariah recorded it, or Matthew refers to the scroll of Jeremiah which included Zechariah.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-11/

- **JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown):** Zechariah connects his prophecy with Jeremiah's older one (the potter's shop scene in Jeremiah 18–19). Matthew quotes Zechariah's words as Jeremiah's because Jeremiah was the original source. Compares Mark 1:2-3 quoting Malachi as "Isaiah."
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/11-13.html (Gill entry citing JFB)

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Suggests Matthew may not have named any prophet; an early transcriber, recalling Jeremiah 32:6-12, may have inserted the name.

## Other Views

### Catholic Reading (Haydock / Challoner / Catholic Encyclopedia)

The Catholic tradition follows a typological approach consistent with much Protestant interpretation (the chapter foreshadows Christ's rejection), but with several distinctive emphases:

- Lebanon = the temple (built of its cedars), citing Josephus on the miraculous opening of the temple gates. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html)
- The two staves = God's gentleness and severity, or general providence and particular care of the Jews — not grace and unity as in most Protestant readings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html)
- The foolish shepherd includes both wicked Jewish leaders and pagan Roman emperors, with Antichrist as ultimate referent. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/zechariah-11.html)
- The Catholic Encyclopedia (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15741b.htm) takes a notably historical-critical approach, seeing the chapter as referring to events surrounding the 586 BC fall of Jerusalem and the wicked kings of Jeremiah's era (Sellum, Joakim, Jechonias for the three shepherds; Zedekiah as the foolish shepherd). This is a minority view that does not read the chapter as primarily messianic.
